claims.title: Forged settlement webhook can mark an order paid if callback authentication is absent
claims.description: `flow:entity:card-processor>process:storefront-api>settlement-webhook` is a public-internet-to-DMZ boundary crossing that carries a settlement confirmation which `process:storefront-api` uses to mark an order paid. Its `authentication` state is unknown. If verification of the card processor's callback is absent or ineffective, an outside attacker can submit a fabricated settlement callback through that flow and cause `process:storefront-api` to accept an unpaid order as paid. This is conditional on the unresolved authentication attribute, not an assertion that webhook verification is missing.

quotes.text: I would have to check how that callback is authenticated.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium and conditional because an internet-side caller can reach the boundary-crossing webhook, but `unknown:flow:entity:card-processor>process:storefront-api>settlement-webhook:authentication` leaves callback verification unresolved. Impact is high because the callback changes payment state for an order, a financial asset handled by `process:storefront-api` and persisted by the order-capture path.

mitigations.summary: Authenticate and verify processor settlement callbacks
mitigations.detail: Require a processor-specific signed webhook scheme on `flow:entity:card-processor>process:storefront-api>settlement-webhook`, verify the signature before changing payment state, and reject callbacks that lack a valid signature.

mitigations.summary: Bind callbacks to expected payment state
mitigations.detail: Have `process:storefront-api` verify the order identifier, processor transaction identifier, amount, and allowable payment-state transition before accepting a settlement event.

claims.title: A compromised DMZ workload can inject orders into the unauthenticated order-service call
claims.description: `flow:process:storefront-api>process:order-service>submit-order` crosses from the storefront DMZ into core services and has authentication stated absent; `process:order-service` accepts submissions without authenticating their sender. An attacker controlling `process:storefront-api` or another workload that can reach the order service can inject crafted order submissions directly into `process:order-service`, bypassing the expected storefront-origin check. The order service can then persist altered or fabricated order contents through `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders` and write corresponding receipts to `store:receipt-archive`.

quotes.text: There is no auth on that gRPC call — the order service accepts anything that can reach it

severity.justification: Likelihood is low because `process:order-service` is internal and exploitation requires control of a component or workload able to reach it, although `absent:flow:process:storefront-api>process:order-service>submit-order:authentication` adds no sender-verification barrier. Impact is high because fabricated submissions can be committed to `store:orders-db`, which holds confidential PII and financial order data.

mitigations.summary: Require service authentication for order submission
mitigations.detail: Use mTLS or workload identity on `flow:process:storefront-api>process:order-service>submit-order` and configure `process:order-service` to accept submissions only from the authorized storefront workload.

mitigations.summary: Validate order provenance and state transitions
mitigations.detail: Have `process:order-service` validate that each submission is bound to an authenticated shopper session and an expected order lifecycle before persisting it.

claims.title: A leaked application-account password enables direct rewriting of all order records
claims.description: `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders` uses one application account with full read/write authority, and its password is stored in an environment variable on `process:order-service`. An attacker who obtains that static password can connect as the application account and alter rows in `store:orders-db` directly, bypassing validation performed by `process:order-service`. The corruption reaches all consumers that read orders through the order-service path and can cause later receipts written to `store:receipt-archive` to reflect altered order data as legitimate.

quotes.text: a single application account that has full read/write. The password comes from an environment variable on the worker.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium because the static application-account password held in the worker environment must first be obtained, but then directly grants the full read/write authority recorded by `assertion:authorization-grant~principal:application-account~s.96924e46de53~v.527ec0f9b94c`. Impact is high because `store:orders-db` is confidential and contains PII and financial order records, allowing broad and authoritative corruption.

mitigations.summary: Replace the static database password with workload identity
mitigations.detail: Authenticate `process:order-service` to `store:orders-db` using short-lived workload-federated credentials rather than a reusable password stored in an environment variable.

mitigations.summary: Restrict the database account's write authority
mitigations.detail: Replace the blanket full read/write grant with least-privilege roles limited to the tables and statements required by `process:order-service`; separate read and write identities where feasible.

mitigations.summary: Detect and constrain direct record changes
mitigations.detail: Use database-side auditing and integrity-sensitive change controls for order and payment fields so direct writes are attributable and anomalous updates can be detected.

claims.title: Offline modification of orders database media is possible if at-rest protection is absent
claims.description: `store:orders-db` holds confidential order records, shopper addresses, and card last-four values, but its `encryption_at_rest` state is unknown. If the store's snapshots, backups, or decommissioned media are not protected with encryption and integrity controls, an attacker holding a storage copy can modify order records offline and have the altered copy restored or reintroduced as authentic. `process:order-service` then consumes the tampered records through `flow:process:order-service>store:orders-db>read-write-orders`. This is conditional on resolution of `store:orders-db` at-rest protection; it does not assert that encryption is absent.

severity.justification: Likelihood is low and conditional because an attacker must obtain a storage copy and `unknown:store:orders-db:encryption_at_rest` does not establish whether at-rest protection exists. Impact is high because the affected store is classified confidential and contains PII and financial order data whose corruption can be consumed again by `process:order-service`.

mitigations.summary: Establish and enforce protected storage for orders data
mitigations.detail: Confirm the at-rest protection of `store:orders-db`, then use managed envelope encryption covering database storage, backups, and snapshots with tightly controlled keys.

mitigations.summary: Verify integrity before restoring data copies
mitigations.detail: Require authenticated backups, protected restore workflows, and integrity verification before a snapshot or backup is reintroduced to `store:orders-db`.
